findings.title: hash() is not stable across process restarts/instances, breaking consistent group-to-queue assignment guarantee claimed in docstring
findings.body: get_queue_for_group uses Python's built-in hash() on group_key (a str). Python randomizes string hash seeds per-process (PYTHONHASHSEED) unless explicitly disabled, so the same group_key can map to different queue indices across different consumer processes or restarts. The FixedQueuePool docstring and comments claim 'Each group is consistently assigned to the same queue' - this is only true within a single process's lifetime, not across restarts. While ordering is still preserved within one process (which is likely the actual requirement, since each partition is handled by one process), the comment is misleading, and if any code or operator assumption relies on cross-process group->queue determinism (e.g., comparing queue assignment for debugging) it will be wrong. Should use a stable hash (e.g., hashlib) or document this limitation.

findings.title: get_committable_offsets scans from last_committed+1 every time -- O(n) per call, called every 1s in commit loop, could become costly with large backlogs
findings.body: get_committable_offsets iterates from `start` to `max_offset` every time it's called (every 1 second via _commit_loop). If a queue backs up significantly (e.g., thousands of outstanding offsets due to a slow consumer in one queue), this loop becomes expensive and runs under a per-partition lock, blocking add_offset/complete_offset calls from worker threads for that partition. This could cause lock contention and slow down the whole pipeline when backlog grows, defeating part of the purpose of this PR (handling slow items without clogging).

findings.title: shutdown() doesn't drain/join queues before stopping workers, risking item loss or offsets never completed
findings.body: FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown=True and calls queue.shutdown(immediate=False) then joins with a 5s timeout. If a queue still has many items and the single worker is slow, items remain un-processed when join times out; those offsets are left 'outstanding' and never committed, and in-flight items are simply dropped (no attempt to drain before closing). This could cause messages to be silently skipped on shutdown/rebalance, which is a correctness risk for an at-least-once pipeline relying on this component for commit safety.

findings.title: get_committable_offsets copies/uses live sets without full isolation; potential iteration-while-mutating under lock release points
findings.body: Inside the per-partition lock block, `outstanding = self.outstanding[partition]` is a reference to the live set, and the loop checks membership against it while iterating `all_offsets`. This is read-only within the lock so it's safe here, but `list(self.all_offsets.keys())` taken outside any lock before the per-partition locking could race with a new partition_lock being created concurrently in `_get_partition_lock`, since `partition_locks` dict itself isn't guarded by a single lock (setdefault is not atomic against concurrent reads elsewhere). This is a subtle concurrency hazard worth flagging even if currently unlikely to manifest.

findings.title: max_workers=None silently defaults to 20 queues with no metric tag differentiation
findings.body: For thread-queue-parallel mode, `num_queues=max_workers or 20` is used, but unlike the batched-parallel mode's metric_tags handling (which distinguishes 'default' vs explicit worker count), there is no equivalent tracking of whether queue count was explicitly set or defaulted for thread-queue-parallel mode. This makes it harder to debug/monitor the chosen parallelism from metrics tags, an inconsistency with the existing batched-parallel code path directly above.
